newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Split on east Zaire laid bare as suffering worsens.
newsitem.headline: Split on east Zaire laid bare as suffering worsens.

text.p: The divisions among world powers about the crisis in eastern Zaire were laid bare on Saturday, further delaying action to help millions of suffering Hutu refugees and Zairean civilians.

The United Nations Security Council withheld backing for a French-sponsored plan for military intervention, telling U.N. members to "lay the groundwork" instead for a multinational force to feed the hungry.
The inaction in New York enraged those warning of catastrophe unless food, water and medicine is rushed to the refugees and east Zaireans caught up in a three-week rebellion.

"Those governments who have prevented the immediate authorisation of a multinational protection force should explain to their citizens and the world why," European Commissioner Emma Bonino thundered in Brussels.
But diplomats said the United States, Britain and Russia all had grave reservations about the French-backed plan.
"What are the intentions? What are you going to do? Who are the bad guys and how are you going to separate them from the good guys?" asked a senior diplomat in central Africa.

In Goma, the biggest east Zaire city captured by rebels in a growing insurrection against President Mobutu Sese Seko, Red Cross officials predicted catastrophe and some 120 exhausted, hungry refugees arrived after walking for more than a week.
Rioting Zaireans seized the last food from a U.N. warehouse in Goma on Friday.
A German aid mission brought some hope on Saturday, delivering the first medical supplies to reach Goma since rebels captured the city just over a week ago in a battle which left about 500 dead.
Dr Jo Lusi, the only surgeon working in Goma, told reporters a combination of lack of food, water and medicine and the spectre of cholera could spell disaster for the region.
"If the cholera begins to do its job, the people will see that the war did not do much," he warned.
Mobutu, a cancer patient in Europe for the past three months, insisted in his first interview he was recovering well.
For the first time he said Zaire accepted a "de facto truce" with the rebels to allow the refugees to be repatriated.
His shaky government in Kinshasa says Mobutu will be back at the helm within days but he told the French daily newspaper Liberation he would convalesce in France for "several weeks".

Fighting in eastern Zaire has spread death, fear and misery across a vast stretch of the biggest country in Central Africa. Hundreds of thousands of Zaireans are also on the move and food is increasingly scarce.

Rwanda and the rebels it supports have both rejected any French role in a multinational force, citing France's long alliances with Mobutu and the former Rwandan Hutu leaders who ordered the genocide of minority Tutsis in 1994.
Rwanda's backing for any move to help the needy is vital. The only other corridor is through Zaire which says the 1.2 million Hutu refugees from Rwanda and Burundi must leave.
But the Hutus have refused to return to their homelands for more than two years, fearing reprisals for the genocide and a bleak future as an underclass below the Tutsis.

Sketchy plans for military intervention, also backed by Spain, fail to explain how the tens of thousands of former Rwandan soldiers and Interahamwe militiamen will be separated from the ordinary Hutu refugees.
These armed men played the leading role in the genocide and face execution or life imprisonment if they return to Rwanda.
A senior diplomat in the region told Reuters western governments were looking at a non-military intervention, getting aid to local people in eastern Zaire's main towns.
But even if rebels in charge of those areas honour pledges to assist, the next daunting step would be to reach the scattered refugees and coerce them back to Rwanda and Burundi.
As the planning drags on, the death toll is rising.
Most of the suffering is far from the reach of journalists. The last aid workers fled eastern Zaire on November 2. Aid agencies are warning of huge loss of life but their estimates are guesswork.
"There were people who died of thirst and exhaustion on the way, but we did not see anybody with any traces of cholera yet," said Charles Kairwa, a 32-year-old Hutu refugee.
He was one of 120 Rwandans who arrived in Goma on Saturday after walking for more than a week without food or water except what they could scavenge by the roadside.
The Security Council's "interim resolution" told U.N. Secretary-General Boutros Boutros-Ghali to draw up a "concept of operations and framework for a humanitarian task force" by November 20.
In what many diplomats interpreted as an attack on the rebels and Rwanda, Boutros spoke of "genocide by starvation" in eastern Zaire two years after the genocide by Hutus.
